question_text: In a △ABC, show that r₁ + r₂ + r₃ − r = 4R.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.
formula_note: One of three near-identical identities. Here the minus sign is on r itself, not an ex-radius, so (r₁ + r₂) + (r₃ − r) collapses to 4R sin((A+B+C)/2) = 4R sin90° = 4R, with no cosine. When an ex-radius carries the minus instead — r + r₁ + r₂ − r₃, or r + r₃ + r₁ − r₂ — the answer is 4R cos(that angle).

steps.label: Group into two pairs
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Group (r₁ + r₂) and (r₃ − r), so each pair shares a factor — 4R cos(C/2) for the first, 4R sin(C/2) for the second.
steps.memory_tip: Group (r₁ + r₂) and (r₃ − r), so each pair shares a factor — cos(C/2) then sin(C/2).

steps.why: Pair each ex-radius sum with the difference that shares a half-angle: (r₁ + r₂) and (r₃ − r) both carry C/2. (r₁ + r₃) and (r₂ − r), around B/2, would work the same way.

steps.label: Apply the compound formulas
steps.margin_note: The other half. The first bracket is sin((A+B)/2) and the second cos((A+B)/2); the compound formula combines them into one sine of (A+B+C)/2, which is 90°.
steps.memory_tip: The two combine into 4R sin((A+B+C)/2) = 4R sin 90° = 4R.

recall.must_convey: That the brackets become sin((A+B)/2) and cos((A+B)/2), which combine to sin((A+B+C)/2) = sin90° = 1.

steps.why: A + B + C = 180° in any triangle, so half of it is 90° and its sine is exactly 1. That is why the answer is a clean 4R with no angles left in it.

insider_note: Group as (r₁ + r₂) and (r₃ − r). The two brackets then combine into one sine of (A+B+C)/2 = 90°, so the answer is simply 4R.
